claim: During replicative aging of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a challenge to proteostasis occurs specifically in the fraction of cells with decreased stability within the ribosomal DNA (rDNA).
source: Using microfluidics and single-cell imaging approaches, we observed that, during the replicative aging of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a challenge to proteostasis occurs specifically in the fraction of cells with decreased stability within the ribosomal DNA (rDNA).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations using microfluidics and single-cell imaging, as stated in the abstract.

claim: A screen of 170 yeast RNA-binding proteins identified ribosomal RNA (rRNA)-binding proteins as the most enriched group that aggregate upon a decrease in rDNA stability induced by inhibition of Sir2.
source: A screen of 170 yeast RNA-binding proteins identified ribosomal RNA (rRNA)-binding proteins as the most enriched group that aggregate upon a decrease in rDNA stability induced by inhibition of a conserved lysine deacetylase Sir2.
evidence: The claim is based on a systematic screen of 170 RNA-binding proteins using the yTRAP system, as described in the abstract and Results section.

claim: Loss of rDNA stability induces age-dependent aggregation of rRNA-binding proteins through aberrant overproduction of rRNAs.
source: Further, loss of rDNA stability induces age-dependent aggregation of rRNA-binding proteins through aberrant overproduction of rRNAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that excessive rRNA production leads to rRNA-binding protein aggregation, as detailed in the Results section.

claim: rRNA-binding protein aggregates contribute to age-induced proteostasis decline and limit cellular lifespan.
source: These aggregates contribute to age-induced proteostasis decline and limit cellular lifespan.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that overexpression of rRNA-binding proteins shortens lifespan in Mode 1 cells, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Yeast replicative aging is characterized as the finite number of cell divisions before cell death.
source: Yeast replicative aging is characterized as the finite number of cell divisions before cell death (Mortimer and Johnston, 1959).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mortimer and Johnston, 1959.

claim: The instability of ribosomal DNA (rDNA), driven by decreased rDNA silencing, was among the first to be identified as a causal factor of yeast aging.
source: In particular, the instability of ribosomal DNA (rDNA), driven by decreased rDNA silencing, was among the first to be identified as a causal factor of yeast aging (Defossez et al., 1999; Li et al., 2017; Saka et al., 2013; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction, driven by early-life decreases in vacuolar acidity and intracellular heme level, was identified as a major contributor to yeast aging.
source: Furthermore, mitochondrial dysfunction, driven by early-life decreases in vacuolar acidity and intracellular heme level, was also identified as a major contributor to yeast aging (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012; Li et al., 2020; Veatch et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: rDNA instability and mitochondrial dysfunction are mutually exclusive in individual aging cells.
source: Adding to these observations, our recent single-cell analyses revealed that rDNA instability and mitochondrial dysfunction are mutually exclusive in individual aging cells.
evidence: The claim is based on single-cell analyses from previous work by the authors.

claim: About half of aging cells show loss of rDNA stability and nucleolar decline, whereas the other half experience mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: In an isogenic population, about half of aging cells show loss of rDNA stability and nucleolar decline, whereas the other half experience mitochondrial dysfunction (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2020.

claim: Hsp104-GFP forms aggregates (visualized as fluorescent foci) upon proteotoxic stress.
source: To track the challenges to proteostasis in single aging cells, we monitored Hsp104-GFP, a canonical protein stress reporter that forms aggregates (visualized as fluorescent foci) upon proteotoxic stress (Lum et al., 2004; Tkach and Glover, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies establishing Hsp104-GFP as a proteotoxic stress reporter.

claim: Yeast cells form Hsp104-GFP foci during aging, and the frequency of such appearance increases with age.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Andersson et al., 2013; Erjavec et al., 2007; Saarikangas and Barral, 2015), yeast cells form Hsp104-GFP foci during aging, and the frequency of such appearance increases with age.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and is consistent with the authors' observations.

claim: Hsp104-GFP foci appear in only a fraction of aging cells, not universally in all aging cells.
source: However, we noticed that Hsp104-GFP foci did not appear universally in all aging cells. Instead, only a fraction of cells showed foci formation during aging (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mode 1 aging is driven by loss of rDNA stability and is characterized by continuous production of elongated daughter cells at the late stages of lifespan.
source: Mode 1 aging is driven by loss of rDNA stability and is characterized by continuous production of elongated daughter cells at the late stages of lifespan.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work by the authors defining Mode 1 aging.

claim: Mode 2 aging retains rDNA stability and is associated with production of small round daughters.
source: In contrast, Mode 2 aging retains rDNA stability and is associated with production of small round daughters (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2020.

claim: Hsp104-GFP forms foci almost exclusively in Mode 1 aging cells, but rarely in Mode 2 cells.
source: We classified a population of aging cells into Mode 1 and Mode 2 (see Figure 1, 'Materials and methods,' and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and found that Hsp104-GFP form foci almost exclusively in Mode 1 aging cells, but rarely in Mode 2 cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—videos 1; 2), indicating that a challenge to proteostasis occurs specifically in Mode 1 aging.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ∆ssCPY*-GFP formed aggregates specifically in Mode 1 aging cells.
source: Consistent with the observed pattern of Hsp104-GFP aggregation, ∆ssCPY*-GFP formed aggregates specifically in Mode 1 aging cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sir2 encodes a conserved lysine deacetylase that mediates chromatin silencing and stability at rDNA.
source: To test this possibility, we deleted SIR2, which encodes a conserved lysine deacetylase that mediates chromatin silencing and stability at rDNA (Gartenberg and Smith, 2016), in the Hsp104-GFP reporter strain.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gartenberg and Smith, 2016.

claim: A dramatically larger fraction of cells showed Hsp104 foci formation in the short-lived sir2Δ mutant compared to WT.
source: We found that, compared to WT, a dramatically larger fraction of cells showed Hsp104 foci formation in the short-lived sir2Δ mutant with loss of rDNA stability (Fritze et al., 1997; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and a citation to Fritze et al., 1997.

claim: Hsp104 foci were formed earlier in life and persisted for a larger portion of the lifespan in sir2Δ cells than in WT cells.
source: In addition, these foci were formed earlier in life and persisted for a larger portion of the lifespan in sir2Δ cells than those in WT cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There is a correlation between the time of first foci appearance and the final lifespan in WT and sir2Δ cells.
source: We further observed a correlation between the time of first foci appearance and the final lifespan in WT and sir2Δ cells, suggesting that the proteostasis stress, indicated by Hsp104 foci formation, contributes to cell aging and death (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The hap4Δ strain is short-lived due to mitochondrial defects but has enhanced rDNA stability.
source: Moreover, to exclude the possibility that sir2Δ exacerbates Hsp104 aggregation simply because it is short-lived, we monitored Hsp104 foci formation during the aging process in the hap4Δ strain, which is short-lived due to mitochondrial defects but has enhanced rDNA stability (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2020.

claim: The hap4Δ strain showed strikingly decreased Hsp104 foci formation compared to WT.
source: We observed strikingly decreased Hsp104 foci formation compared to WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Deletion of SIR2 in the hap4Δ strain had a modest effect on the lifespan, but substantially increased Hsp104 foci formation.
source: Deletion of SIR2 in the hap4Δ strain had a modest effect on the lifespan, but substantially increased Hsp104 foci formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B), confirming the role of Sir2 in protecting from proteostasis stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Sis1 is an Hsp40 co-chaperone and a reporter for nuclear proteostatic stress.
source: To determine whether proteostasis in the nucleus is similarly challenged during aging, we monitored mNeon-tagged Sis1, an Hsp40 co-chaperone and a reporter for nuclear proteostatic stress (Feder et al., 2021; Klaips et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Feder et al., 2021 and Klaips et al., 2020.

claim: Sis1-mNeon formed sharp foci predominantly in WT Mode 1 aging cells.
source: We found that Sis1-mNeon formed sharp foci predominantly in WT Mode 1 aging cells (Figure 1C) and exhibited earlier and more frequent foci formation in sir2Δ cells (Figure 1D), in agreement with Hsp104 aggregation during aging.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Sis1-mNeon exhibited earlier and more frequent foci formation in sir2Δ cells.
source: We found that Sis1-mNeon formed sharp foci predominantly in WT Mode 1 aging cells (Figure 1C) and exhibited earlier and more frequent foci formation in sir2Δ cells (Figure 1D), in agreement with Hsp104 aggregation during aging.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: rDNA instability can serve as a contributing factor for age-associated challenges to proteostasis.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that rDNA instability can serve as a contributing factor for age-associated challenges to proteostasis.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental results presented.

claim: Sir2, by maintaining rDNA silencing, represses age-dependent protein aggregation.
source: Sir2, by maintaining rDNA silencing, represses age-dependent protein aggregation, consistent with the role of sirtuins in alleviating protein aggregation-induced cytotoxicity and disorders (e.g., Huntington disease), in yeast and mammalian models (Cohen et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2011; Kobayashi et al., 2005; Sorolla et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: A disproportionately high number of RNA-binding proteins contain low complexity, prion-like domains and hence are aggregation-prone.
source: A disproportionately high number of RNA-binding proteins contain low complexity, prion-like domains and hence are aggregation-prone (Calabretta and Richard, 2015; Kato et al., 2012; Weber and Brangwynne, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The yTRAP RNA-binding protein sensor library is composed of 170 unique sensor strains, encompassing every known RNA-binding protein with an experimentally confirmed physical interaction with RNAs in yeast.
source: The yTRAP RNA-binding protein sensor library is composed of 170 unique sensor strains, encompassing every known RNA-binding protein with an experimentally confirmed physical interaction with RNAs in yeast (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim describes the composition of the yTRAP library used in the screen.

claim: When RNA-binding proteins are in a soluble unaggregated state, the sensor GFP fluorescence is high; however, if the RNA-binding protein enters an aggregated state, the GFP fluorescence is reduced.
source: When RNA-binding proteins are in a soluble unaggregated state, the sensor GFP fluorescence is high; however, if the RNA-binding protein enters an aggregated state, the GFP fluorescence is reduced (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim describes the mechanism of the yTRAP system.

claim: Nicotinamide (NAM) is a commonly used inhibitor of Sir2.
source: To conditionally trigger a loss of Sir2 activity, we exposed cells to nicotinamide (NAM), a commonly used inhibitor of Sir2 (Bitterman et al., 2002; Kato and Lin, 2014; Orlandi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NAM treatment induced elongated cell morphology, rDNA silencing loss, and increased Hsp104 aggregation.
source: The NAM treatment induced elongated cell morphology, rDNA silencing loss (indicated by a constantly high rDNA-GFP signal) (Li et al., 2017), and increased Hsp104 aggregation (Figure 2B and C), recapitulating the aged phenotypes in sir2∆ and in the late phases of Mode 1 aging.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Of the 170 RNA-binding proteins tested, 43 Responders displayed at least a 50% decrease in the normalized fluorescence signal upon the NAM treatment.
source: Of the 170 RNA-binding proteins tested on our screen (Figure 2E, left, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), we identified 43 Responders, which displayed at least a 50% decrease in the normalized fluorescence signal upon the NAM treatment (Figure 2E, middle, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and 15 Responders with a more than 75% decrease in the normalized fluorescence signal (Figure 2E, right, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the screen shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 15 Responders showed a more than 75% decrease in the normalized fluorescence signal upon NAM treatment.
source: Of the 170 RNA-binding proteins tested on our screen (Figure 2E, left, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), we identified 43 Responders, which displayed at least a 50% decrease in the normalized fluorescence signal upon the NAM treatment (Figure 2E, middle, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and 15 Responders with a more than 75% decrease in the normalized fluorescence signal (Figure 2E, right, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the screen shown in Figure 2E.

claim: From both Responder groups, there was a consistent and striking enrichment of rRNA-binding proteins involved in rRNA processing.
source: From both Responder groups, we found a consistent and striking enrichment of rRNA-binding proteins involved in rRNA processing.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the screen results.

claim: The absence of Sir2 expression promoted aggregation of all five rRNA-binding proteins tested (Nop15, Sof1, Rlp7, Nop13, Mrd1).
source: We showed that the absence of Sir2 expression promoted aggregation of all five rRNA-binding proteins tested (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), confirming the specificity of aggregation to loss of Sir2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: rRNA-binding proteins in young cells are uniformly localized along one side of the nucleus, forming a single crescent shape, characteristic of the yeast nucleolus.
source: We observed that the rRNA-binding proteins in young cells are uniformly localized along one side of the nucleus, forming a single crescent shape, characteristic of the yeast nucleolus.
evidence: The claim is based on confocal microscopy observations.

claim: At the late stages of aging, most rRNA-binding proteins formed multiple irregular-shaped coalescences or condensates in Mode 1 aged cells.
source: At the late stages of aging, most rRNA-binding proteins formed multiple irregular-shaped coalescences or condensates (visualized as fluorescent patches or foci) in Mode 1 aged cells.
evidence: The claim is based on confocal microscopy observations shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In Mode 2 aged cells, rRNA-binding proteins remained in the uniform crescent shape like that of young cells.
source: In contrast, in Mode 2 aged cells, these rRNA-binding proteins all remained in the uniform crescent shape like that of young cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Age-dependent condensation led to a partial loss of colocalization of rRNA-binding proteins (e.g., Nop13 and Nop15).
source: We also observed that age-dependent condensation led to a partial loss of colocalization of rRNA-binding proteins (e.g., Nop13 and Nop15; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which may be indicative of a deterioration of their coordinated functions in rRNA processing and ribosomal biogenesis in the nucleolus.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sis1 clearly accumulated in Nop15 condensates in aged cells, whereas no such colocalization was observed in young cells.
source: We found that Sis1 clearly accumulated in Nop15 condensates in aged cells, whereas no such colocalization was observed in young cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Age-induced rRNA-binding protein condensates are bona fide protein aggregates and contribute to the challenges to nuclear proteostasis observed during aging.
source: These results indicate that age-induced rRNA-binding protein condensates are bona fide protein aggregates and contribute to the challenges to nuclear proteostasis observed during aging (as visualized by Sis1 foci; Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the colocalization of Sis1 with rRNA-binding protein condensates.

claim: Twofold overexpression of each rRNA-binding protein significantly shortened the lifespan of Mode 1 aging cells.
source: For each of the rRNA-binding proteins tested, we observed consistently that twofold overexpression of each significantly shortened the lifespan of Mode 1 aging cells, but not that of Mode 2 aging cells in the same isogenic population (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Twofold overexpression of rRNA-binding proteins did not shorten the lifespan of Mode 2 aging cells.
source: For each of the rRNA-binding proteins tested, we observed consistently that twofold overexpression of each significantly shortened the lifespan of Mode 1 aging cells, but not that of Mode 2 aging cells in the same isogenic population (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The aggregated form of rRNA-binding proteins causes cell deterioration and limits cellular lifespan in Mode 1 cells.
source: These results indicate that the aggregated form (in Mode 1 cells) of these rRNA-binding proteins causes cell deterioration and limits cellular lifespan, whereas increasing the non-aggregated form (in Mode 2 cells) shows either no effect or a small extension of the lifespan.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the differential effects of overexpression in Mode 1 vs Mode 2 cells.

claim: Nop15 functions in 60S ribosomal biogenesis.
source: We selected Nop15, which functions in 60S ribosomal biogenesis, as a representative to investigate the pathways and factors that regulate rRNA-binding protein aggregation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Nop15 function.

claim: Nop15 formed aggregates during aging of WT cells, with the frequency and severity increasing with age.
source: We observed that Nop15 formed aggregates during aging of WT cells, with the frequency and severity increasing with age (Figure 4A) and following changes in rDNA copy number (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: RNA-binding proteins, many of which contain intrinsically disordered domains, are frequent substrates of proteasomal degradation.
source: Recent studies have shown that RNA-binding proteins, many of which contain intrinsically disordered domains, are frequent substrates of proteasomal degradation (Myers et al., 2018; Thapa et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Rpn4 is a transcriptional regulator of the 26S proteasome components that is required for normal levels of proteasome activity.
source: To examine the effects on rRNA-binding protein aggregation, we began with Rpn4, a transcriptional regulator of the 26S proteasome components that is required for normal levels of proteasome activity (Xie and Varshavsky, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Xie and Varshavsky, 2001.

claim: Cells lacking Rpn4 are characterized by a reduced proteasome pool.
source: In cells lacking Rpn4, which are characterized by a reduced proteasome pool (Ju et al., 2004; Xie and Varshavsky, 2001), we found increased, earlier, and more severe Nop15 aggregation during aging (Figure 4B, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cells lacking Rpn4 showed increased, earlier, and more severe Nop15 aggregation during aging.
source: In cells lacking Rpn4, which are characterized by a reduced proteasome pool (Ju et al., 2004; Xie and Varshavsky, 2001), we found increased, earlier, and more severe Nop15 aggregation during aging (Figure 4B, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ubr2 is a ubiquitin ligase that mediates Rpn4 degradation.
source: In contrast, deletion of UBR2, which encodes a ubiquitin ligase that mediates Rpn4 degradation, leads to elevated proteasome capacity (Wang et al., 2004) and thereby dramatically alleviated Nop15 aggregation (Figure 4B, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2004.

claim: Deletion of UBR2 leads to elevated proteasome capacity and dramatically alleviated Nop15 aggregation.
source: In contrast, deletion of UBR2, which encodes a ubiquitin ligase that mediates Rpn4 degradation, leads to elevated proteasome capacity (Wang et al., 2004) and thereby dramatically alleviated Nop15 aggregation (Figure 4B, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and a citation to Wang et al., 2004.

claim: The proteasome participates in the process of removing age-induced rRNA-binding protein aggregates.
source: These results suggest that the proteasome participates in the process of removing age-induced rRNA-binding protein aggregates, probably through degradation of intrinsically disordered protein monomers as in the case of other misfolded protein aggregates or aberrant RNA-binding protein aggregates (Berke and Paulson, 2003; Brown and Kaganovich, 2016; Hjerpe et al., 2016; Reiss et al., 2020; Thapa et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on experimental results and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deletion of Sir2 promotes much earlier and more frequent appearance of Nop15 aggregation during aging.
source: Consistently, we observed much earlier and more frequent appearance of Nop15 aggregation during aging of sir2Δ cells (Figure 4C, left), indicating that deletion of Sir2 or loss of rDNA stability promotes rRNA-binding protein aggregation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The yeast rDNA contains 100–200 tandemly arrayed copies of a 9.1 kb rDNA repeat, coding for rRNA subunits of ribosomes.
source: The yeast rDNA contains 100–200 tandemly arrayed copies of a 9.1 kb rDNA repeat, coding for rRNA subunits of ribosomes.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about yeast rDNA structure.

claim: During aging, loss of silencing at the rDNA enhances the rate of DNA double-strand breaks and recombination, leading to the formation of extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs).
source: During aging, loss of silencing at the rDNA enhances the rate of DNA double-strand breaks and recombination (Lindstrom et al., 2011; Saka et al., 2013), leading to the formation of extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs) excised from this fragile genomic site.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ERCs are self-replicating DNA circles, asymmetrically segregated to mother cells during cell division.
source: ERCs are self-replicating DNA circles, asymmetrically segregated to mother cells during cell division.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ERCs.

claim: ERCs accumulate exponentially in aging mother cells and have been proposed to be a causal factor of aging.
source: As a result, ERCs accumulate exponentially in aging mother cells and have been proposed to be a causal factor of aging (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sinclair and Guarente, 1997.

claim: Fob1 is a replication fork-barrier protein that, when deleted, prevents rDNA recombination and abolishes ERC formation.
source: To determine whether loss of Sir2 or loss of rDNA stability drives rRNA-binding protein aggregation through ERC accumulation, we monitored Nop15 aggregation in the absence of Fob1, a replication fork-barrier protein that, when deleted, prevents rDNA recombination and abolishes ERC formation (Defossez et al., 1999; Johzuka and Horiuchi, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A dramatic reduction in Nop15 aggregation was observed in the fob1∆ strain.
source: We observed a dramatic reduction in Nop15 aggregation in the fob1∆ strain, indicating that ERC accumulation can be a major driver of age-dependent rRNA-binding protein aggregation (Figure 4C, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ERC accumulation can be a major driver of age-dependent rRNA-binding protein aggregation.
source: We observed a dramatic reduction in Nop15 aggregation in the fob1∆ strain, indicating that ERC accumulation can be a major driver of age-dependent rRNA-binding protein aggregation (Figure 4C, right).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental observation that fob1∆ reduces Nop15 aggregation.

claim: ERC accumulation dramatically increases the number of transcriptionally active rDNA copies, resulting in a massive increase in pre-rRNA levels in the nucleolus.
source: A recent study showed that ERC accumulation dramatically increases the number of transcriptionally active rDNA copies, resulting in a massive increase in pre-rRNA levels in the nucleolus. These pre-rRNAs, however, cannot mature into functional ribosomes (Morlot et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Morlot et al., 2019.

claim: Pre-rRNAs produced from ERCs cannot mature into functional ribosomes.
source: A recent study showed that ERC accumulation dramatically increases the number of transcriptionally active rDNA copies, resulting in a massive increase in pre-rRNA levels in the nucleolus. These pre-rRNAs, however, cannot mature into functional ribosomes (Morlot et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Morlot et al., 2019.

claim: Increasing the level of RNA content generally promotes phase transition and aggregation of ribonucleoprotein complexes.
source: Because increasing the level of RNA content generally promotes phase transition and aggregation of ribonucleoprotein complexes (Lin et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015), we hypothesized that excessive production of rRNAs could induce age-dependent aggregation of rRNA-binding proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Rrn3 is the RNA Pol I-specific transcription factor that promotes rRNA transcription.
source: To test this, in the fob1Δ mutant where ERC formation is abolished, we overexpressed Rrn3, the RNA Pol I-specific transcription factor that promotes rRNA transcription (Moorefield et al., 2000; Philippi et al., 2010; Yamamoto et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Excessive rRNA production by Rrn3 overexpression is sufficient to induce Nop15 aggregation in the absence of ERCs.
source: In support of our hypothesis, we observed that the excessive rRNA production by Rrn3 overexpression is sufficient to induce Nop15 aggregation in the absence of ERCs (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Age-dependent loss of rDNA stability promotes rRNA-binding protein aggregation through ERC accumulation and excessively high levels of rRNAs transcribed from ERCs.
source: Taken together, these results revealed that age-dependent loss of rDNA stability promotes rRNA-binding protein aggregation through ERC accumulation and, more specifically, excessively high levels of rRNAs transcribed from ERCs.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of the experimental results presented.

claim: rRNA-binding protein aggregation may impair the normal function of rRNA-binding proteins in pre-rRNA processing and maturation and the assembly of functional ribosomes.
source: This aggregation may impair the normal function of rRNA-binding proteins in pre-rRNA processing and maturation and the assembly of functional ribosomes, accounting for the decoupling of rRNA transcription and ribosomal biogenesis during aging (Morlot et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the experimental results and supported by a citation.

claim: Increased expression and aggregation of intrinsically disordered proteins impose an increased burden on protein folding resources and the proteasome, leading to global proteostasis decline.
source: Previous studies showed that increased expression and aggregation of intrinsically disordered proteins impose an increased burden on protein folding resources and the proteasome, leading to global proteostasis decline (Andersson et al., 2013; Bence et al., 2001; Outeiro and Lindquist, 2003; Stefani and Dobson, 2003; Verhoef, 2002; Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is continuous co-occurrence of Nop15 aggregation and Hsp104 foci during the later stage of aging in the majority of Mode 1 cells.
source: We found continuous co-occurrence of Nop15 aggregation and Hsp104 foci during the later stage of aging in the majority of Mode 1 cells (Figure 5A, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In 66% of Mode 1 cells, Nop15 aggregation immediately preceded the co-occurrence phase with Hsp104 foci.
source: Furthermore, in 66% of these cells, Nop15 aggregation (indicated by green bars in Figure 5A) immediately preceded the co-occurrence phase (indicated by yellow bars in Figure 5A), suggesting that rRNA-binding protein aggregation leads to global proteostasis stress in a large fraction of aging cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: rRNA-binding protein aggregation leads to global proteostasis stress in a large fraction of aging cells.
source: Furthermore, in 66% of these cells, Nop15 aggregation (indicated by green bars in Figure 5A) immediately preceded the co-occurrence phase (indicated by yellow bars in Figure 5A), suggesting that rRNA-binding protein aggregation leads to global proteostasis stress in a large fraction of aging cells.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the temporal relationship between Nop15 aggregation and Hsp104 foci appearance.

claim: Deletion of SIR2 promotes proteostasis stress during aging, as reflected by increased Hsp104 foci formation.
source: In further support of the causal connection from rRNA-binding protein aggregation to proteostasis stress, the deletion of SIR2, which reduces rDNA stability and enhances rRNA-binding protein aggregation (Figure 4C, left), promotes proteostasis stress during aging, as reflected by increased Hsp104 foci formation (Figures 1B and 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 5B.

claim: Deletion of FOB1 showed dramatically decreased Hsp104 foci formation.
source: In contrast, the deletion of FOB1, which enhances rDNA stability and reduces rRNA-binding protein aggregation (Figure 4C, right), showed dramatically decreased Hsp104 foci formation (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Overexpression of Rrn3 in the fob1Δ mutant increased Hsp104 foci formation.
source: To test whether elevated rRNA-binding protein aggregation can impact proteostasis independent of ERCs, in the fob1Δ mutant where ERC formation is abolished, we overexpressed Rrn3 and Nop15, respectively, as both perturbations can enhance rRNA-binding protein aggregation. We observed increased Hsp104 foci formation, indicating that elevated rRNA-binding protein aggregation is sufficient to induce proteostasis stress (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, compare fob1∆ + RRN3 o/e and fob1∆ + NOP15 o/e with fob1∆ alone).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Overexpression of Nop15 in the fob1Δ mutant increased Hsp104 foci formation.
source: To test whether elevated rRNA-binding protein aggregation can impact proteostasis independent of ERCs, in the fob1Δ mutant where ERC formation is abolished, we overexpressed Rrn3 and Nop15, respectively, as both perturbations can enhance rRNA-binding protein aggregation. We observed increased Hsp104 foci formation, indicating that elevated rRNA-binding protein aggregation is sufficient to induce proteostasis stress (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, compare fob1∆ + RRN3 o/e and fob1∆ + NOP15 o/e with fob1∆ alone).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Elevated rRNA-binding protein aggregation is sufficient to induce proteostasis stress.
source: We observed increased Hsp104 foci formation, indicating that elevated rRNA-binding protein aggregation is sufficient to induce proteostasis stress (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, compare fob1∆ + RRN3 o/e and fob1∆ + NOP15 o/e with fob1∆ alone).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental results showing that overexpression of Rrn3 or Nop15 in fob1Δ increases Hsp104 foci.

claim: Deletion of UBR2 substantially extended the lifespan of the HAP4 O/E strain.
source: We found that deletion of UBR2, which increases proteasome capacity and alleviates rRNA-binding protein aggregation and proteostasis burden (Figure 3B), substantially extended the lifespan of the HAP4 O/E strain (Figure 6B), in support of a working model in which proteostasis stress is a major contributing factor to Mode 1 aging driven by rDNA instability.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Proteostasis stress is a major contributing factor to Mode 1 aging driven by rDNA instability.
source: We found that deletion of UBR2, which increases proteasome capacity and alleviates rRNA-binding protein aggregation and proteostasis burden (Figure 3B), substantially extended the lifespan of the HAP4 O/E strain (Figure 6B), in support of a working model in which proteostasis stress is a major contributing factor to Mode 1 aging driven by rDNA instability.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental results showing that alleviating proteostasis stress extends lifespan in Mode 1 cells.

claim: Overexpression of Hsp104 can dramatically extend the lifespan of sir2Δ, but not WT cells.
source: For instance, it has been puzzling why overexpression of Hsp104, a disaggregase that clears protein aggregation, can dramatically extend the lifespan of sir2Δ, but not WT cells (Erjavec et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Erjavec et al., 2007.

claim: Only a fraction of WT cells (Mode 1) experience chromatin instability and proteostasis decline at late stages of aging.
source: Based on our results, only a fraction of WT cells (Mode 1) experience chromatin instability and proteostasis decline at late stages of aging and therefore the effect of Hsp104 overexpression on lifespan is rather modest.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' experimental results.

claim: The majority of sir2Δ cells age with accelerated and severe rRNA-binding protein aggregation and proteostasis decline due to sustained loss of chromatin stability.
source: In contrast, the majority of sir2Δ cells age with accelerated and severe rRNA-binding protein aggregation and proteostasis decline due to sustained loss of chromatin stability.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' experimental results.

claim: In C. elegans, age-dependent changes in epigenetic landscape and chromatin accessibility lead to a repression of the heat-shock response (HSR) that combats protein misfolding, resulting in proteostasis decline.
source: For example, in C. elegans, age-dependent changes in epigenetic landscape and chromatin accessibility lead to a repression of the heat-shock response (HSR) that combats protein misfolding, resulting in proteostasis decline (Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015.

claim: During human cell senescence, the losses of silencing and repression on transposon and satellite repeat activation cause disorganized nuclear distribution of HSF1, contributing to HSR suppression and proteostasis decline.
source: During human cell senescence, the losses of silencing and repression on transposon and satellite repeat activation cause disorganized nuclear distribution of HSF1 (the central transcription factor that mediates HSR), contributing to HSR suppression and proteostasis decline (Gaglia et al., 2020; Jolly et al., 2002; Swanson et al., 2013; Van Meter et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ERC-like DNA circles in yeast cells impair nuclear pore integrity, causing aberrant pre-mRNA nuclear export and translation and consequently contributing to loss of proteostasis.
source: A very recent report showed that ERC-like DNA circles in yeast cells impair nuclear pore integrity, causing aberrant pre-mRNA nuclear export and translation and consequently contributing to loss of proteostasis (Meinema et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meinema et al., 2021.

claim: Multiple different mechanisms may operate in parallel to mediate the interplay between chromatin stability and proteostasis during aging.
source: We speculate that multiple different mechanisms may operate in parallel to mediate the interplay between chromatin stability and proteostasis during aging.
evidence: The claim is a speculation by the authors.

claim: Aberrant formation and persistence of RNA-binding protein aggregates have been found to contribute to degenerative diseases, including multi-system proteinopathy, Paget's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, frontotemporal lobar degeneration, and Alzheimer's disease.
source: For example, aberrant formation and persistence of RNA-binding protein aggregates have been found to contribute to degenerative diseases, including multi-system proteinopathy, Paget's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, frontotemporal lobar degeneration, and Alzheimer's disease, making RNA-binding protein aggregates promising therapeutic targets for treating degenerative diseases (Khalil et al., 2018; Li et al., 2013; Ramaswami et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The yTRAP system couples protein aggregation states to fluorescent reporter output.
source: In this study, we took advantage of a recently developed synthetic genetic system, yTRAP, which couples protein aggregation states to fluorescent reporter output (Newby et al., 2017), and a high-throughput microfluidic platform, DynOMICS, which enables simultaneous time-lapse measurements of a large number of fluorescent strains over an extended period of time (Graham et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Newby et al., 2017.

claim: The DynOMICS platform enables simultaneous time-lapse measurements of a large number of fluorescent strains over an extended period of time.
source: In this study, we took advantage of a recently developed synthetic genetic system, yTRAP, which couples protein aggregation states to fluorescent reporter output (Newby et al., 2017), and a high-throughput microfluidic platform, DynOMICS, which enables simultaneous time-lapse measurements of a large number of fluorescent strains over an extended period of time (Graham et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Graham et al., 2020.

claim: The screen identified a number of mRNA-binding proteins that aggregate upon loss of Sir2 activity.
source: In addition to the rRNA-binding proteins, our screen has also identified a number of mRNA-binding proteins (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on the screen results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: mRNA-binding proteins bind to mRNAs and form ribonucleoprotein complexes, which play important roles in post-transcriptional control of gene expression and a wide array of physiological functions.
source: These proteins bind to mRNAs and form ribonucleoprotein complexes, which play important roles in post-transcriptional control of gene expression and a wide array of physiological functions (Buchan, 2014; Chakravarty et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2020; Lee and Lykke-Andersen, 2013; Mitchell and Parker, 2014; Ramaswami et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The yeast RBP Whi3 forms aggregates during aging, resulting in sterility in aged yeast cells.
source: For example, previous studies showed that the yeast RBP Whi3 forms aggregates during aging, resulting in sterility in aged yeast cells (Schlissel et al., 2017).

source: In particular, proteins involved in pre-mRNA splicing are highly enriched (Figure 2E) and would be of special interest for in-depth analyses.

claim: Cell aging is a highly dynamic and stochastic process in which isogenic cells age with distinct molecular and phenotypic changes, and thereby markedly different lifespans.
source: Furthermore, it has been increasingly recognized that cell aging is a highly dynamic and stochastic process in which isogenic cells age with distinct molecular and phenotypic changes, and thereby markedly different lifespans.

claim: Recent advances in single-cell technologies provide enabling tools for tracking the aging processes of a large number of individual cells and defining the core aging networks that govern the fate and dynamics of deterioration in aging cells.
source: Recent advances in single-cell technologies provide enabling tools for tracking the aging processes of a large number of individual cells and defining the core aging networks that govern the fate and dynamics of deterioration in aging cells (He et al., 2020; OLaughlin et al., 2020).
